clinical: The recurrent laryngeal nerves ascend in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus, through the loose tissue of this layer. Injury to them during thyroid surgery can paralyse one vocal fold and cause hoarseness.

Cartilage.description: The C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings keep the windpipe open, and the trachealis muscle bridges the open back wall where the rings do not meet. Hyaline cartilage has no blood supply, so its chondrocytes, which sit in small spaces called lacunae, are fed by diffusion from the perichondrium.
clinical: Weak tracheal cartilage lets the airway collapse when breathing out, causing noisy breathing or wheeze. It can be present from birth or develop later, for example after prolonged mechanical ventilation.
A narrowed windpipe can follow prolonged intubation or a tracheostomy, where cuff pressure damages the rings and the healing scar narrows the lumen.

Mucosa & submucosa.description: The lamina propria is loose connective tissue just under the lining, packed with lymphocytes, IgA plasma cells, mast cells and capillaries. The submucosa lies deeper, holding the seromucous glands and larger blood vessels, and elastic fibres give the airway wall its springy recoil.
clinical: In asthma the lamina propria and submucosa swell and fill with inflammatory cells, which narrows the airway and makes breathing out difficult.

Glands.description: Mucous glands in the submucosa, most numerous in the back wall and between the rings, make sticky mucus that traps dust and microbes. Serous cells capping each tubule add watery fluid containing lysozyme and secretory IgA, and ducts carry the secretion through the lining to the surface.
clinical: Hypertrophy of these mucous glands raises mucus output and causes a productive cough. Clinically, chronic bronchitis means a cough with sputum on most days for at least three months in each of two successive years.
A faulty CFTR chloride channel in these cells leaves the secretion thick and dehydrated, so mucus clogs the airways and clearance fails.

Epithelium.description: The lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: every cell touches the basement membrane, but only the tall ciliated and goblet cells reach the lumen, so the nuclei look scattered at different heights. Beating cilia sweep the mucus blanket upward, and short basal cells at the base act as stem cells that renew the lining.
clinical: Inherited defects in the cilia's dynein arms impair their beating, so mucus is not cleared and sinus infections and bronchiectasis follow. When the organs are also reversed left to right (situs inversus), the combination is called Kartagener syndrome.
Long-term cigarette smoke destroys cilia, increases goblet cells and can change the lining to flat squamous cells (squamous metaplasia), so mucus builds up and clears poorly.

parts.description: The adventitia is the outermost layer of the tracheal wall, a loose sheath of connective tissue that binds the trachea to the oesophagus behind and to the thyroid gland and neck structures in front. It carries the blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics that supply the airway, including the tracheal branches of the inferior thyroid arteries. In a section it is the loose, fibrous outer layer lying outside the cartilage rings and trachealis, and it blends into surrounding tissue without a sharp boundary.

The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue lying between the respiratory epithelium and the submucosa, forming the core of the airway mucosa. It contains a rich network of capillaries and many defence cells, including lymphocytes, IgA-secreting plasma cells (antibody-producing cells) and mast cells, and it often holds lymphoid nodules. In a section it is the pale, cell-rich zone directly beneath the basement membrane.

The basement membrane is the sheet of extracellular matrix that separates the respiratory epithelium from the lamina propria and anchors the epithelial cells to it. In the trachea and bronchi it is relatively thick, because a dense subepithelial layer, the lamina reticularis, is made chiefly of type III collagen. In asthma this layer thickens further through subepithelial fibrosis, and in a PAS-stained section the whole membrane shows as a sharp magenta band just beneath the epithelium.

Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium is the columnar lining of the trachea and most of the conducting airways. Every cell rests on the basement membrane, but the basal cells never reach the lumen, so the nuclei lie at different levels and the single layer looks stratified. Besides ciliated and goblet cells, it contains basal stem cells, brush cells and neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells. Chronic irritation, such as cigarette smoke, can convert it to stratified squamous epithelium, a process called squamous metaplasia.

The territorial matrix is the darker, strongly basophilic ring of matrix that immediately surrounds each isogenous group of chondrocytes in hyaline cartilage. It is rich in sulphated proteoglycans, which bind basic dyes such as haematoxylin, so it stains more deeply than the paler interterritorial matrix lying between the groups. Recognising it helps you see that each isogenous group came from a single parent chondrocyte that divided and then secreted this capsule around its daughter cells.

Lacunae are the small cavities in the cartilage matrix in which individual chondrocytes sit. Each lacuna is the space that the cell occupies within the matrix it has secreted, and in life the cell almost fills it, so the lacuna closely follows the cell's shape. In a fixed H&E section the chondrocyte shrinks away from the lacunar wall during processing, leaving a clear halo that looks like an empty gap but is a common artefact.

The submucosa is the layer of looser connective tissue lying between the lamina propria and the cartilage rings. It holds the seromucous glands, the larger blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics of the airway wall, and it merges with the perichondrium around the rings. In a section it is recognised by its looser texture and by the clusters of gland acini and ducts that lie within it.

Mucous tubules are the mucus-secreting parts of the submucosal glands in the trachea, and they are lined by pale, columnar mucous cells. They make much of the sticky mucus that traps dust and microbes on the airway surface, and the tubules drain through ducts to the lumen. In a section, the mucous cells look pale and clear in H&E and stain strongly with PAS (periodic acid–Schiff) because of their mucin.

Serous demilunes are crescent-shaped caps of serous cells that sit over the mucous tubules, while serous acini are rounded secretory units made of serous cells alone. Serous cells are pyramid-shaped, with a round nucleus near the base and cytoplasm full of dense secretory granules, so in H&E they look darker than the pale mucous cells beside them. Their watery secretion contains lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls, and secretory IgA, an antibody that defends the airway surface.

Gland ducts are the narrow passages that carry secretions from the submucosal tubules and acini to the surface of the airway. They are lined by simple cuboidal or low columnar epithelium, and they open through the surface epithelium into the lumen. In a section, look for small, round channels with a neat cuboidal lining, lying among the larger gland units in the submucosa.

Arterioles are the small muscular branches that supply the trachea, derived from the tracheal branches of the inferior thyroid arteries. They run in the adventitia, enter the wall between the cartilage rings, and send twigs into the submucosa, the glands and a dense subepithelial capillary plexus. In a section, look for small round vessels with a thick smooth-muscle wall and a narrow lumen, which sets them apart from the thin-walled venules beside them.

Venules are the small, thin-walled vessels that collect blood from the trachea's capillaries and pass it on to larger veins. Those in the trachea drain into the inferior thyroid veins, and a dense subepithelial venous plexus lies just beneath the surface epithelium. Warm blood flowing through this plexus helps to warm and humidify the air as it is breathed in. In a section, venules look like wide-lumened vessels with a very thin wall and little smooth muscle.

In the trachea, elastic fibres form a dense band called the elastic membrane in the deep lamina propria, at the border with the submucosa. The fibres are made of elastin, which lets the airway wall stretch and then recoil. In a section, elastic fibres stain dark with Weigert's or Verhoeff's stains, and they show up as wavy dark lines marking the boundary between mucosa and submucosa.

Goblet cells are unciliated, mucus-secreting cells scattered among the ciliated cells of the respiratory epithelium. Each has a flask-shaped body with an apical theca, a cap packed with MUC5AC mucin granules that stain pale in H&E and strongly PAS-positive. Their mucus gel traps inhaled particles and floats on the watery periciliary layer that bathes the cilia. Goblet cells multiply in smokers, in asthma and in chronic bronchitis, so the mucus layer thickens.

Cilia are hair-like, motile projections from the apical surface of ciliated cells, each with a 9+2 axoneme of nine outer doublets around two central microtubules. Dynein arms slide these microtubules past one another to bend the cilium, and neighbouring cilia beat in coordinated waves that sweep the mucus blanket towards the larynx, the mucociliary escalator. In primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome), faulty dynein arms cause chronic chest and sinus infections.

Ciliated cell nuclei are the oval nuclei of the tall ciliated cells, which lie in the middle and upper part of the epithelium. Their cell bodies reach from the basement membrane up to the lumen, but the basal cell nuclei sit lower, against the basement membrane, so the nuclei lie at different levels. This two-tier arrangement in a single layer of cells is what makes the epithelium 'pseudo'-stratified.

Basal cells are small, triangular-shaped stem cells that sit on the basement membrane and never reach the airway lumen. They divide to renew the ciliated and goblet cells, and they anchor the epithelium to the basement membrane with hemidesmosomes (protein junctions that grip the matrix). In a section, look for a row of small, rounded nuclei along the basement membrane, beneath the taller columnar cells.

The basement membrane beneath the respiratory epithelium has two parts, the basal lamina and the reticular layer below it. The basal lamina is a thin, dense sheet of type IV collagen and laminin secreted by the epithelial cells, and the epithelial cells are attached to it by hemidesmosomes. The reticular layer of fine collagen fibres underneath gives the lining a firm base, so the epithelium is not torn away from the wall.

Ciliated cells are the tall, column-shaped cells that make up a large share of the respiratory epithelium, and each carries many cilia on its free apical surface. Their bases rest on the basement membrane, and their apical ends reach the airway lumen, where the cilia beat to move mucus upwards. In a section, they are recognised by a fringed apical border and by nuclei that lie in the middle and upper part of the epithelium.

The body of a ciliated cell is the cytoplasm that fills the column between its base on the basement membrane and its apical surface. The apical part is packed with basal bodies, which anchor the cilia, and with many mitochondria that supply the energy for ciliary beating. Neighbouring cells are sealed to one another by tight junctions near the lumen, which keep the airway lining watertight.

Ciliated cell nuclei are oval and usually paler than the small, round basal cell nuclei beneath them. Because the ciliated cells are tall and their nuclei sit at varying heights, the nuclei appear staggered rather than lying in a neat single row. To identify them in a section, look for oval nuclei in the middle and upper epithelium, with the darker basal nuclei pressed against the basement membrane below.

Goblet cells are the mucus-secreting cells that sit in the surface layer of the epithelium, wedged between the tall ciliated cells, with their apical ends reaching the lumen and their bases resting on the basement membrane. They have no cilia, and their apex carries short microvilli instead. In a section, they are spotted by their pale, clear cytoplasm and their mucus-filled, flask-shaped apex.

The body of a goblet cell is the narrow stalk that runs from the basement membrane up to the swollen, mucus-filled apex. Its cytoplasm contains plenty of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, the organelles that make and package mucin. As the apex fills, the nucleus is squeezed down to the base of the cell.

Goblet cell nuclei are small and compressed, and they are pushed to the base of each cell by the mucus that fills the apex. Because they lie low in the epithelium, they often sit at a lower level than the oval nuclei of the neighbouring ciliated cells. In a section, a goblet cell is identified by its clear cytoplasm above a small, low-lying nucleus.

The body of a basal cell is the scanty, pale cytoplasm of the small triangular cells that form the lowest layer of the epithelium. Each basal cell is joined to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes and to its neighbours by desmosomes, so the layer stays firmly attached. Because they never reach the lumen, basal cells are seen only at the base of the epithelium.

Basal cell nuclei are small and round, and they lie in the lowest row of the epithelium, directly on the basement membrane. They form a neat row along the base of the epithelium, which is a useful landmark for finding the base of the lining in a section. Their cells are the stem population that renews the epithelium.

Goblet cell mucus is the mucin stored as secretory granules in the apical theca of each goblet cell before it is released. Once discharged, the granules swell and mix with water to form a viscous gel, which becomes the upper layer of the airway's mucus blanket. In a section, the stored mucin looks pale in H&E but stains strongly magenta with PAS.

Cilia are hair-like, motile projections that grow only from the apical surface of ciliated cells, and goblet cells on the same surface carry none. Each cilium projects into the periciliary layer, a thin watery fluid that lets it beat freely beneath the mucus gel. In a section, the cilia form a fine fringe along the apex that identifies a ciliated cell.

Each cilium is a hair-like, motile projection anchored by a basal body, a modified centriole sitting just beneath the apical membrane of a ciliated cell. A ciliary rootlet, a fibrous rod, extends from the basal body deep into the apical cytoplasm and holds the cilium firmly in place. Together the basal body and rootlet let the cilium withstand the repeated bending of each beat.

The gland duct wall is the thin layer of cells and connective tissue that encloses the lumen of each duct as it runs from a submucosal gland to the surface. The inner lining is a single layer of cuboidal or low columnar cells resting on a basement membrane, and a thin sheath of connective tissue with small blood vessels lies outside it. In a section, a duct wall appears as a small ring with a narrow, regular lumen, beside the larger gland units.

Each cell lining a gland duct is cuboidal, with a round central nucleus, and its cytoplasm can change the ionic makeup of the secretion as it passes towards the surface. Neighbouring duct cells are joined by junctional complexes that seal the duct, so the secretion cannot leak into the surrounding connective tissue. In a section, duct cells look smaller and more uniform than the secretory cells of the acini.

The mucous gland wall is the wall of the mucous tubules, formed by mucous secretory cells resting on a basement membrane. Outside the secretory cells lie flattened myoepithelial cells, which contract to squeeze mucus out of the gland towards its duct. Loose connective tissue of the submucosa surrounds the whole unit and carries its blood supply.

Each mucous cell has pale cytoplasm packed with mucin droplets, and its flattened nucleus is pressed against the basement membrane at the base. Neighbouring mucous cells are sealed to one another by junctional complexes near the tubule lumen, which keep mucus inside the gland and tissue fluid out. In a section, mucous cells are recognised by their clear, foamy cytoplasm and the flattened nuclei at their bases.
